title: Family & people
goal: Talk about your family, say whose something is, and use masculine/feminine nouns and their plurals.
intro:
Family is at the centre of Indian life, and Hindi has a word for every relative — your father's brother and your mother's brother are different people with different names!

In this unit you'll meet two essentials of Hindi grammar: **gender** (every noun is masculine or feminine) and **possession** with का/की/के, which behaves like an adjective.

phrases.native: मेरे परिवार में चार लोग हैं।
phrases.roman: mere parivār meṃ chār log haiṃ.
phrases.en: There are four people in my family.
How many brothers and sisters do you have?

phrases.native: मेरे दो भाई हैं और एक बहन है।
phrases.roman: mere do bhāī haiṃ aur ek bahan hai.
phrases.en: I have two brothers and one sister.

phrases.native: जी हाँ, मेरी शादी हो गई है।
phrases.roman: jī hāṃ, merī shādī ho gaī hai.
phrases.en: Yes, I'm married. (lit. my wedding has happened)

phrases.native: नहीं, अभी मेरी शादी नहीं हुई।
phrases.roman: nahīṃ, abhī merī shādī nahīṃ huī.

phrases.en: How many children do you have?

phrases.roman: hamāre do bachche haiṃ — ek beṭā aur ek beṭī.
phrases.en: We have two children — a son and a daughter.

phrases.native: यह मेरी दादी की फ़ोटो है।
phrases.roman: yah merī dādī kī foṭo hai.
phrases.en: This is a photo of my grandmother.

grammar.title: Gender and plural of nouns
grammar.body:
Every Hindi noun is **masculine** or **feminine**. For people it follows sex; for things you must learn it (this course marks it m/f). Two endings are good clues: **-ā** is usually masculine (लड़का, कमरा), **-ī** is usually feminine (लड़की, कुर्सी) — but there are exceptions (आदमी 'man' is m., पानी 'water' is m.).

Plurals (when the noun is the subject, with no postposition after it) follow four patterns:

**m. ending in -ā** → -e: लड़का → लड़के, बेटा → बेटे
**other m.** → no change: भाई → भाई, आदमी → आदमी, घर → घर
**f. ending in -ī** → -iyāṃ: लड़की → लड़कियाँ, बेटी → बेटियाँ
**other f.** → -eṃ: बहन → बहनें, औरत → औरतें, माँ → माँएँ

Respected relatives ending in -ā (पिता, चाचा, मामा, दादा) **don't change** in the plural.

grammar.title: Possession: का / की / के and मेरा / मेरी / मेरे
grammar.body:
'Amit's brother' is **अमित का भाई** — literally 'Amit of brother'. The postposition **का** comes after the owner, and it changes its ending to agree with the **thing owned** (not the owner!):

**का** before a masculine singular noun: अमित **का** भाई
**की** before any feminine noun: अमित **की** बहन, अमित **की** बहनें
**के** before a masculine plural noun (or a respected person): अमित **के** भाई (Amit's brothers)

Possessive pronouns work exactly the same way: मेरा / मेरी / मेरे 'my', हमारा 'our', तुम्हारा 'your (familiar)', आपका 'your (respectful)', उसका 'his/her', उनका 'their / his/her (respectful)'.

So **उसका भाई** can mean 'his brother' or 'her brother' — the -ā ending only tells you भाई is masculine.

For 'I have (relatives)', Hindi just says 'my two brothers are': **मेरे दो भाई हैं**.

dialogue.title: The family photo
dialogue.setting: Neha visits her friend Priya and sees a framed photo on the wall. They are friends, so they use तुम.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.native: ये मेरे पापा हैं, और ये मेरी मम्मी।
lines.roman: ye mere pāpā haiṃ, aur ye merī mammī.
lines.en: This is my dad, and this is my mum.

lines.speaker: Neha
lines.native: और यह लड़का? तुम्हारा भाई है?
lines.roman: aur yah laṛkā? tumhārā bhāī hai?
lines.en: And this boy? Is he your brother?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.native: हाँ, यह मेरा छोटा भाई है। उसका नाम रोहन है।
lines.roman: hāṃ, yah merā chhoṭā bhāī hai. uskā nām Rohan hai.
lines.en: Yes, this is my younger brother. His name is Rohan.

lines.speaker: Neha
lines.en: Do you have a sister too?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.native: हाँ, एक बड़ी बहन है। उसकी शादी हो गई है।
lines.roman: hāṃ, ek baṛī bahan hai. uskī shādī ho gaī hai.
lines.en: Yes, an older sister. She's married.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.native: ये उसके बच्चे हैं — एक बेटा और एक बेटी।
lines.roman: ye uske bachche haiṃ — ek beṭā aur ek beṭī.
lines.en: These are her children — a son and a daughter.

culture: Hindi kinship terms are precise: चाचा (father's younger brother), ताऊ (father's elder brother), मामा (mother's brother), मौसी (mother's sister), बुआ (father's sister) — each with a matching spouse term. Strangers are addressed as family too: a shopkeeper or driver is **भैया**, a young woman **दीदी**, an older man or woman **अंकल** / **आंटी** (from English), and elders **चाचा जी** or **माता जी**. Using a first name alone for someone older can sound rude. Many Indians grow up in a **joint family** (संयुक्त परिवार), with grandparents, uncles and cousins under one roof, and cousins are often simply called भाई and बहन.
